final:
**Evening, the Long Shadow**

I've finished the painting. It's an invented late-summer evening in the manner of Inness's later work. A big oak grove fills the left side, nearly one dark mass against a warm, hazy sky. A single small gap under its canopy shows a strip of far, sunlit field. The low sun sits behind three young trees on the right, and the grove's long shadow lies over the meadow toward us. A small woman in a red shawl stands just where that shadow meets the gold light. She is the only warm accent in an olive, umber and violet-grey setting, beneath a soft blue ridge and a cream-to-mauve sky.

I painted it as he worked: a linen canvas stained with raw umber and sienna, a thin rubbed-in umber lay-in, then many separate sessions over paint that had dried, with glazes and soft blending between them.

Some parts aren't as I wanted. The three young trees are too crisp and round, the far gold strip of field is a little loud, and the grove's leaf edge on the left looks cut out against the sky. I stopped there rather than push further. Fixing small areas on dry paint kept leaving visible seams, and only repainting whole areas wet held together.

final:
I've finished the painting and called it **Evening, the Long Shadow**.

A big grove of dark elms takes up the left side, its edges dissolving into a warm, hazy evening sky. Under it there's one small gap where you can see the far lit fields. The grove's shadow runs diagonally across the meadow toward the viewer and joins the warm brown foreground, and that one big dark shape holds the picture together. To the right, three young trees stand against the pale lemon light near the horizon, with a blue-violet ridge and a soft line of woods behind them. A small figure in a red shawl stands right where the shadow meets the light, and it's the only strong colour in the picture.

**This last session:**
- **Young trees:** I redrew their crowns as three separate trees with a gap of sky between the two tall ones. Each crown is darker on the inner side and warmer olive toward the sun.
- **Trunks:** I made them thicker and darker, down to their feet in the grass.
- **Grove's left edge:** I repainted it as dark leaves breaking into the sky, so it no longer looks cut out.

**What's still wrong:**
- **Gold strip:** the far gold field is still a little too insistent. I tried two thin glazes to calm it, but both left grey bars, so I wiped them off and left the strip as it was.
- **Edge marks:** at the far left edge of the sky there are two very faint marks left from colour tests, which I covered as well as I could.

Most of my repairs on dry paint here left a visible seam, so I stopped rather than push either of these further.

final:
**Evening, the Edge of the Grove**

I looked over the painting again today, whole and with a squint. I'm leaving it as it was when I called it finished.

It's a late-day pastoral in Inness's manner. A big dark grove of oaks stands against a warm, hazy sky that goes from violet-grey at the top to a lemon glow low on the right. Its long shadow lies across the meadow toward us, so the left half of the picture is one large dark L. Three young trees stand backlit against the glow, in front of a far blue ridge and a strip of gold field. Through one gap under the grove's canopy you can see a bit of distant light. The only warm accent is a small figure in a red shawl, standing right where the grove's shadow meets the sunlit grass.

Some faults remain. The young trees' crowns are a little crisp, the far gold strip draws too much attention, and the lit meadow on the right is somewhat flat. Every time I tried a local repair on dry paint in this painting, it left a visible seam, so I've stopped while the large shapes still hold together.
